summary: Describes the notations for writing a text string as a Dial Sequence, made of DTMF tones plus separators and actions such as waiting for dial tone or pausing, needed to reach a target telephone service. It covers subaddresses and menu navigation. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Dialing a phone can include pauses and waiting for tones. This memo defines a way to write all of that as plain text.

questions: what does p and w mean in a phone number string
what is a gstn phone string
subtitle: A single text notation for phone numbers, pauses, waits and menu key presses.

tldr.problem: Many specifications need to write down a telephone number or a whole sequence of keypresses as text, and each could invent its own way of doing so.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines one ABNF grammar. A phone-string is made of DTMF keys, pause (p), tone wait (w) and readability separators (- and .). Global numbers start with +, and local numbers, subaddresses and post-dial sequences reuse the same pieces.
tldr.outcome: It collects definitions already used in other Standards Track specifications, and says it MUST be used by other specifications that need a text form of a Dial Sequence.

today: RFC 3601 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by any later RFC.

sections.title: Why a Dial Sequence Notation
sections.content:
Since the first devices that talked to telephone services appeared, there has been a need for one text representation of telephone numbers and, more generally, of DTMF sequences and the actions around them. This memo describes that representation. It was written to be an easy, unique and complete reference that MUST be used by all other specifications needing a text string for a Dial Sequence.

Nothing here is new invention. The notation was collected from Dial Sequence definitions already in Standards Track specifications such as RFC 3191, RFC 3192, RFC 2846 and RFC 2806, and is described as fully synchronized with them.

It does not cover everything in a phone address. Full abstract E.164 addresses have elements that cannot be dialled, so they cannot be fully converted to a Dial Sequence with this notation.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of programs need to write down phone numbers and button presses. This memo picks one way so they all agree.

sections.title: Terms and Syntax Conventions
sections.content:
Formal definitions use ABNF (RFC 2234) and some of its core definitions. Requirement words follow RFC 2119.

The memo defines these terms: a Dial Sequence is a series of DTMF elements and human or device actions; a phone-string is its text form; a GSTN address is what is commonly called a telephone number, meaning a diallable subset of an E.164 abstract address or any diallable private numbering address; gstn-phone is its text form; subaddr-string is the text form of a GSTN subaddress, including ISDN and T.33 subaddresses; and post-dial is the text form of a post dialling sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using the new words, the memo lists what each one means, like a small dictionary at the start of a game.

sections.title: The phone-string Building Block
sections.content:
A Dial Sequence has three kinds of element. DTMF elements are the keys on a numeric keypad. Actions are performed by the agent, human or device, composing the sequence. Separators exist only to make it easier for people to read.

The grammar is phone-string = 1*( DTMF / pause / tonewait / written-sep ). A DTMF element is a digit, the hash and asterisk keys, or the letters A, B, C or D. The letters apply only to DTMF operations, not to the letters mapped to digits on keypads in some countries. The pause action is p, the tonewait action is w, and the separators (written-sep) are the hyphen and the full stop.

The exact meaning of pause and tonewait depends on the device and is not mandated. As common practice, one pause SHOULD be read as a pause of one second. A tonewait SHOULD be read as a pause until the caller hears a dial tone or another sign that more characters may be processed, and an off-hook indication MAY count as such a sign. Characters after either one SHOULD be sent with DTMF signalling. Both are case insensitive.

Separators MUST NOT cause any action, and conforming implementations MAY drop or insert them.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone-string is a recipe of button presses. The letter p means count to one and wait. The letter w means wait for the beep. Dashes and dots are only there to make it easier to read.

sections.title: Global and Local Phone Numbers
sections.content:
A gstn-phone is either a global-phone or a local-phone. This lets the notation cover diallable E.164 numbers as well as local or private addressing schemes.

A global-phone represents a diallable E.164 numeric address: a leading + followed by one or more digits or separators. The + is strictly reserved for this form, and no other dialling scheme may use a leading +.

A local-phone covers cases where the global form does not apply. It is an optional exit-code followed by a dial-number, or an exit-code followed by an optional dial-number. Both are phone-strings. The exit code can hold things such as the digit to reach an outside line, a carrier access code or an access password. The dial number can hold the local number, area code and country code where needed. A local-phone MUST NOT contain +, and it MUST NOT be empty.
sections.plainLanguage: A number starting with a plus sign is the worldwide kind. Anything else is a local kind, which may start with extra digits like the one you press to get an outside line.

sections.title: Subaddresses and Post-Dial Sequences
sections.content:
Sometimes a subaddress is needed to reach the final destination. A subaddr-string is simply a phone-string. Specific services may narrow it: ISDN subaddresses limit the elements to digits and separators, and the fax T.33 subaddress limits them to digits only.

A post-dial is also a phone-string. It is used after the connection is made, when more dialling is needed to reach further services, for example an automated menu driven by DTMF.
sections.plainLanguage: After the phone connects you sometimes still press more buttons, like choosing options in a voice menu. Those later presses use the same notation.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives examples for illustration. 01139040226338 is an Italian address dialled from the U.S.A. as a local-phone without separators. +49.81.7856345 is a German global-phone with full stop separators, and +1-202-455-7622 is a U.S. global-phone with hyphen separators.

The post-dial sequence pppp1w7005393w373 pauses, dials 1, waits for dial tone, dials 7005393, waits again and dials 373; the four p elements make a longer initial pause. In 9p040p22.63.38, 9 is the exit code, 0 is the long distance access, 40 is the area code, and the letter p is a pause and the full stop is a separator. The last example, 0w00800-39380023pp334422p1234, has exit code 0, a wait for dial tone, an international 800 toll-free number dialled from Belgium with prefix 00, then a post-dial sequence entering the user ID 334422 and the PIN 1234 for a voice mailbox.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show real-looking strings, such as a number with dashes or one with pauses in the middle, and explain what each part does.

sections.title: Security of Codes in Dial Strings
sections.content:
Dial Sequences can include private codes such as Personal Identification Numbers used to reach special services. Because these text strings could be carried unencoded inside protocols or applications, unauthorized people might get hold of the codes.

Users SHOULD be given ways to prevent this disclosure, such as encrypting the codes or masquerading techniques. The RFC lists out-of-band communication of authorization information, or encrypted data in special fields, as the available non-standard techniques.
sections.plainLanguage: If a secret code is written into the text, anyone who reads the text can see it. So the secret part should be hidden or sent a safer way.

viz.caption: COLLECTED ABNF FOR DIAL SEQUENCES (RFC 3601, SECTION 9)

data.title: Collected ABNF
data.code:
phone-string = 1*( DTMF / pause / tonewait / written-sep )
DTMF = ( DIGIT / "#" / "*" / "A" / "B" / "C" / "D" )
written-sep = ( "-" / "." )
pause = "p"
tonewait = "w"
gstn-phone = ( global-phone / local-phone )
global-phone = "+" 1*( DIGIT / written-sep )
local-phone =  [ exit-code ] dial-number
local-phone =/ exit-code [ dial-number ]
exit-code = phone-string
dial-number = phone-string
subaddr-string = phone-string
post-dial = phone-string
